title: Heat and Thermodynamics
lines: USAT heat questions test the kinetic theory of gases, the first law of thermodynamics applied to gas processes, specific heats of gases, and heat engines (Carnot efficiency and the second law). Almost every numerical requires temperatures in kelvin, which is where most marks are lost.
## Temperature
- T(K) = t(°C) + 273. Absolute zero is 0 K ≈ −273 °C, where the molecular kinetic energy of an ideal gas would be zero.
- Thermal equilibrium (zeroth law): if A and B are each in equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other. This is what makes a thermometer work.
- Heat energy Q = mcΔT for a temperature change, and Q = mL for a change of state at constant temperature.
## Kinetic theory of gases

Assumptions: a gas consists of a very large number of tiny molecules in random motion, colliding elastically; their own volume is negligible and they do not attract each other except during collisions.
- Pressure: P = ⅓ρ⟨v²⟩, produced by molecules striking the walls.
- Ideal gas equation: PV = nRT = NkT, with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and Boltzmann's constant k = R/Nₐ = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
- Average translational kinetic energy of one molecule = (3/2)kT, which depends only on temperature.
- Root mean square speed v(rms) = √(3RT/M) = √(3kT/m).
> Example 1. A gas is heated from 27 °C to 927 °C. By what factor does its rms speed change?
> In kelvin: 300 K to 1,200 K, four times larger. Since v(rms) ∝ √T, the speed doubles.
- At the same temperature, all gases have the same average molecular kinetic energy, but lighter molecules move faster: hydrogen molecules are four times faster than oxygen molecules.
## Internal energy and the first law
The internal energy U of an ideal gas is the total kinetic energy of its molecules and depends only on temperature.
First law: Q = ΔU + W, where Q is the heat given to the gas and W is the work done by the gas. (Some books write ΔU = Q − W; it is the same law.)
| Process | Condition | First law becomes
| Isothermal | ΔT = 0 | ΔU = 0, so Q = W
| Adiabatic | Q = 0 | W = −ΔU; expansion cools the gas
| Isochoric | ΔV = 0 | W = 0, so Q = ΔU
| Isobaric | ΔP = 0 | Q = ΔU + PΔV
> Example 2. A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. Find the change in its internal energy.
> ΔU = Q − W = 500 − 200 = +300 J. The internal energy rises, so the gas gets hotter.
- Work done by a gas = area under its P-V graph; for a cycle it is the area enclosed.
- An adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal one through the same point (PV^γ = constant against PV = constant).
> Example 3. A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³. Find the work done.
## Molar specific heats
- C(v) is the heat needed per mole per kelvin at constant volume, C(p) at constant pressure.
- C(p) − C(v) = R, and γ = C(p)/C(v).
- Monatomic gases (He, Ar): C(v) = (3/2)R, γ = 5/3. Diatomic gases (N₂, O₂, air): C(v) = (5/2)R, γ = 1.4.
- C(p) is larger because at constant pressure part of the heat does work as the gas expands.
## Heat engines and the second law
A heat engine takes heat Q₁ from a hot source at T₁, does work W and rejects heat Q₂ to a cold sink at T₂.
- Efficiency η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁.
- The Carnot engine (two isothermal and two adiabatic steps) is the most efficient possible between two temperatures: η = 1 − T₂/T₁, with T in kelvin.
- Second law (Kelvin): no engine can turn all the heat it takes in into work. (Clausius): heat does not flow by itself from a cold body to a hot one.
- A refrigerator uses work to move heat from cold to hot. Its coefficient of performance is Q₂/W.
- Entropy change ΔS = ΔQ/T. In every real (irreversible) process the total entropy of the universe increases.
> Example 4. A Carnot engine works between 527 °C and 127 °C. Find its efficiency.
! Never put Celsius temperatures into η = 1 − T₂/T₁ or PV = nRT. 1 − 127/527 gives a wrong 76 %.
! Even a perfect Carnot engine cannot reach 100 % efficiency, because that would need a sink at 0 K.
! In an isothermal change the gas still takes in heat; it is the temperature, not the heat, that stays constant.
## Quick check
- Kelvin temperature doubled: average molecular kinetic energy? (doubled)
- Which process has no heat exchange? (adiabatic)
- Work done in an isochoric process? (zero)
- C(p) − C(v) for one mole of ideal gas? (R)
- Does Carnot efficiency depend on the working substance? (no, only on T₁ and T₂)
